title: Both Schools agree free choice is a faculty, not really distinct from intellect and will; two questions remain
source_text: II. Secundo patet ex iis quae ante fuerunt a nobis exposita, utramque scholam in eo convenire quod liberum arbitrium non sit actus, aut habitus aliquis, sed ad facultates animae pertineat: neque tamen sit facultas quaedam reapse ab intellectu & voluntate distincta. Quae autem hodie de liberi arbitrii in homine natura quaestiones moventur alicujus momenti, ad hasce revocari possunt. Cujus facultatis respectu homo dicatur esse liberi Arbitrii? Deinde, Qua in re sita sit libertas a qua liberum in nobis dicitur arbitrium?
pass_a_gloss: Secondly it is plain from those things which were before set forth by us, that both schools agree in this, that free choice is not an act, or any habit, but pertains to the faculties of the soul: and yet that it is not some faculty really distinct from the intellect and will. But the questions of any moment which are moved today concerning the nature of free choice in man may be brought back to these. In respect of what faculty is man said to be of free Choice? Next, In what thing is that liberty placed from which choice is called free in us?
pass_b_english: Second, what we set out earlier makes it clear that both schools agree that free choice is neither an act nor a habit but belongs among the soul's faculties, and yet is not a faculty really distinct from intellect and will.

The questions of any weight now raised about the nature of man's free choice come down to two. With respect to which faculty is man said to have free choice? And what does the freedom consist in, on account of which our choice is called free?

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
